name: Strawman / Strawperson
definition: Misrepresenting an argument to make it easier to attack by exaggerating, distorting, or simplifying it. This is a fallacy because it avoids engaging with the real issue.
examples: You support private identity verification, so you want everyone's legal name displayed publicly.
You want a person to check the tool's rejections, so you want us to go back to reading 4,000 applications by hand.

name: Ad Hominem (Character attack)
definition: Attacking the person making the argument instead of addressing the argument itself. This is a fallacy because personal traits do not determine the validity of a claim.
examples: You only support this regulation because you dislike technology.
You only defend the hiring tool because you have never been rejected by one.

name: Red Herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the actual issue being debated. It is a fallacy because it distracts from resolving the core problem.
examples: Instead of debating anonymity, we should talk about how much time young people spend on their phones.
Before we discuss whether the tool is fair, think about how tired our three recruiters are.

name: Burden of Proof Shift
definition: Demanding that others disprove your claim instead of providing evidence yourself. It is a fallacy because the responsibility to prove a claim lies with the one making it.
examples: Prove to me that anonymous accounts do not cause harassment.
Show me evidence that the tool rejects good applicants. Until you do, we should assume it is fair.

name: Moving the Goalposts
definition: Changing the criteria for success after they have been met. It is a fallacy because it creates an unfair standard that can never be satisfied.
examples: Even if real-name rules reduce harassment, it doesn't count unless they also stop misinformation.
The tool passed the bias audit, but that doesn't count unless it can also explain every single decision.

name: Whataboutism
definition: Responding to criticism by accusing the other party of hypocrisy. It is a fallacy because it evades addressing the argument itself.
examples: You criticise anonymous accounts, but your own team posts under pseudonyms, so you have no right to object.
You say the tool is biased, but your recruiters were biased too, so you cannot criticise it.

name: False Dilemma
definition: Presenting two options as the only possibilities when others exist. This is a fallacy because it oversimplifies complex issues.
examples: Either we ban anonymity or online harassment will continue unchecked.
Either we use the screening tool or we stop hiring altogether.

name: Slippery Slope
definition: Arguing that a small first step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without evidence. It is a fallacy because it assumes a chain reaction without justification.
examples: Introducing identity verification will inevitably lead to governments monitoring everyone's private conversations.
If we let software sort applications, soon software will decide who gets promoted and who gets fired.

name: Circular Reasoning
definition: Restating the claim instead of providing evidence. It is a fallacy because it assumes the conclusion within the premise.
examples: Anonymity is harmful because posting anonymously does damage.
The tool selects the best applicants because the applicants it selects are the best.

name: Post Hoc (False Cause)
definition: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second. This is a fallacy because correlation does not imply causation.
examples: The platform introduced real names last year and harassment reports fell, so real names caused the drop.
We started using the tool in January and staff turnover fell, so the tool hires better people.

name: Composition/Division
definition: Assuming that what is true for a part is true for the whole, or the reverse. It is a fallacy because parts and wholes can behave differently.
examples: This one forum works well with real names, so every platform should require them.
The tool works well for our sales positions, so it will work well for every position in the company.

name: Faulty Analogy (Overgeneralization from Similarity)
definition: Assuming that because two things share some traits, they are alike in all ways. It is a fallacy because surface similarities do not guarantee deeper equivalence.
examples: Banks check their customers' identity, so social media platforms should check their users' identity too.
A spam filter sorts emails without problems, so a tool can sort job applicants the same way.

name: Cherry-Picking (Attack via Single Example)
definition: Selecting only negative cases to imply an entire system is flawed. This is a fallacy because it ignores the full range of evidence.
examples: This one case of an anonymous account harassing a journalist shows that anonymity is dangerous.
This one strong applicant that the tool rejected shows that the whole system is useless.

name: Appeal to Authority
definition: Claiming something is true because an authority figure says it is, without supporting evidence. It is a fallacy because authorities can be wrong.
examples: A well-known tech CEO says anonymity must end, so it must.
The vendor says the tool is fair, so it is fair.

name: Bandwagon Appeal (Appeal to the Majority)
definition: Claiming something is right or better because many people believe or do it. It is a fallacy because popularity is not proof of truth.
examples: Most large platforms ask for real names, so it must be the right approach.
Most companies our size use AI to screen applicants, so it must be the best way.

name: Appeal to Tradition
definition: Arguing that something is better simply because it has been traditionally done that way. It is a fallacy because longevity does not guarantee effectiveness.
examples: People have always been able to post anonymously online, so we should keep it that way.
Recruiters have always read applications themselves, so we should keep doing it.

name: Appeal to Fear
definition: Using fear to persuade instead of logical reasoning. It is a fallacy because fear alone is not evidence.
examples: If we keep anonymity, your children will be targeted by strangers and nobody will ever be caught.
If we don't adopt the tool, our competitors will hire all the talent and the company will fail.

name: Appeal to Nature
definition: Arguing that something is good or right because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural. It is a fallacy because "natural" does not necessarily mean better.
examples: Speaking under your own name is natural. Hiding behind a username is not how humans are meant to communicate.
Judging people is a naturally human task, so a machine should never do it.

name: Hasty Generalization
definition: Drawing a broad conclusion from a small or unrepresentative sample. It is a fallacy because the evidence is insufficient to support the generalization.
examples: One platform had a data breach, so every identity-verification system will fail.
The tool rejected two good applicants last month, so it always rejects good applicants.

name: Anecdotal Evidence
definition: Using personal stories as proof instead of systematic evidence. It is a fallacy because personal experience does not represent broader reality.
examples: I was harassed by an anonymous account once, so anonymity is what causes harassment.
My cousin was hired through an AI screening tool and she is excellent, so these tools work.

name: No True Scotsman (person)
definition: Dismissing counterexamples by redefining the group or standard. It is a fallacy because it avoids addressing legitimate contradictions.
examples: If a real-name platform still has harassment, it was not really enforcing real names.
If the tool produced unfair results, it was not a real AI screening tool.

name: Genetic Fallacy
definition: Judging a claim based on its origin rather than its merit. It is a fallacy because the truth of an idea is independent of its source.
examples: The proposal to restrict anonymity came from a government ministry, so it cannot be about protecting users.
The tool was built by a start-up, so it cannot be good enough for a serious company.

name: Guilt by Association
definition: Discrediting an idea by associating it with an unpopular group or person. It is a fallacy because an idea's value is not determined by who else believes it.
examples: Authoritarian governments also want to end online anonymity, so we cannot take this proposal seriously.
A company known for mistreating its workers uses this tool, so the tool must be harmful.

name: Moral Licensing
definition: Assuming that previous good actions justify current questionable decisions. It is a fallacy because past achievements do not guarantee good judgment in new situations.
examples: Our platform has done so much for online safety that if we decide to keep anonymous accounts, it must be the right decision.
We have an excellent record on diversity, so if we choose this tool, it must be fair.
